title: Don Quixote — Week 1
sub: The windmill mystery. Four rounds built around Ms. Santos's big question: is Don Quixote simply imagining adventures, or does he believe they are real?
cite: Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes, Core Classics abridged for young readers
note: Everything here comes from pages 1–12, the part you have read. Get one wrong and a hint tells you the page — that page number is what goes in the Cite column of your evidence table.
bigq: Is Don Quixote simply imagining adventures, or does he believe they are real? Use three examples from the reading and explain your judgment.

groups.name: Round 1
groups.blurb: Straight comprehension of pages 1 to 12, so the facts are solid before you argue anything.

groups.name: Round 2
groups.blurb: Every question here is a ready-made row for your evidence table: what he believed, what was really there, and the page.

groups.name: Round 3
groups.blurb: The rules on the toolkit page. What C means, when to use quotation marks, and what counts as a theme.

groups.name: Round 4
groups.blurb: Chivalry, squire and irony — the three words on your Week 1 page.

items.q: Where does the gentleman live?
opts: In a village in the province of La Mancha, in Spain
In the city of Seville, on the southern coast of Spain
In a castle in the mountains above a village in Spain
On a farm in the hills of Portugal, close to the border
items.hint: The very first sentence names the province. He keeps an ancient lance and shield hung up in his hall there.
items.why: “Once upon a time there lived in a village in Spain, in the province of La Mancha.” Later he puts that name into his own.

items.q: What was his name at the start of the story, before he changed it?
opts: Amadis
Rocinante
Quixania
Caraculiambro
items.hint: One short sentence gives it, right after the book says he was about fifty and a great lover of hunting.
items.why: “His name was Quixania.” He invents Don Quixote for himself later on.

items.q: What was he like at the beginning of the story?
opts: A wealthy young lord with a large household of servants, horses and dogs
About fifty, thin but tough, an early riser and a great lover of hunting
A young and strong man who had already been trained as a knight
A soldier who had fought in many real battles for the king
items.hint: He was thin, with a lean face, and he was a very early riser.
items.why: “Our gentleman was about fifty, thin, but tough of body, with a lean face, a very early riser, and a great lover of hunting.”

items.q: What did he sell so that he could buy more books?
opts: His best suit of clothes for Sundays and holidays
The ancient lance and shield from his hall
His hunting dog and his riding horse
Several acres of good cropland
items.hint: He gave up part of the very land his income came from, to buy as many books as he could lay his hands on.
items.why: “He even sold several acres of good cropland in order to buy as many books about chivalry as he could.” A useful piece of evidence: he is already acting on what he reads.

items.q: What did all that reading finally do to him?
opts: It made him a better hunter than he had ever been before
His brain became agitated and his judgment warped
It made him want to write a book of romances of his own
It made him famous among the gentlemen of his village
items.hint: He lost interest in hunting and neglected his daily concerns. The book says what happened to his judgment.
items.why: “His brain became so agitated and his judgment so warped, that he resolved to become a knight himself.”

items.q: What happened when he tested his new cardboard visor?
opts: His sword broke in half against the hard cardboard
He destroyed it with one stroke of his sword
It held up perfectly well and he was delighted
He decided it was too risky and did not test it
items.hint: He wanted to know whether it would resist cuts, so he drew his sword and struck it.
items.why: “He made a stroke at it and in one instant demolished” the work of a whole week.

items.q: What did he name his horse, and how long did it take him to decide?
opts: Bucephalus, after a single day
Rocinante, after four days
Dulcinea, after eight whole days
Amadis, after a whole week
items.hint: The animal was only skin and bone, but he thought it finer than the famous horse of Alexander.
items.why: “He spent four days considering” the matter and “at last fixed on Rocinante.”

items.q: What name did he finally give himself?
opts: Don Belianis of the Steel Cap
Don Quixote de la Mancha
Don Quixote of Toboso
Don Amadis of Gaul and Spain
items.hint: It took him eight days more. He copied the valiant Amadis, who added the name of his country to his own.
items.why: He enlarged it to Don Quixote de la Mancha, so he “made clear his origin and honored his country.”

items.q: When did he set out on his first journey?
opts: At noon in the middle of a cold winter, with snow on the ground
One morning before daybreak, on one of the hottest days in July
On a cool evening in spring, just as the sun was going down
At midnight, during one of the worst storms of the year
items.hint: He went out through a private gate of his yard, so that nobody would see him leave.
items.why: “One morning before daybreak, on one of the hottest days in July, he donned his armor, mounted Rocinante.”

items.q: Which road did Don Quixote take?
opts: The widest and busiest road that he could find
The road leading back toward his own village
The road that led south in the direction of Seville
Whichever road his horse chose
items.hint: He thought that letting it happen this way was the true spirit of adventure.
items.why: “He allowed his horse to follow whatever road it pleased, considering this to be the true spirit of adventure.”

items.q: Don Quixote wanted to lay his armor before the altar in the chapel. Why did he not?
opts: There was no chapel anywhere near the inn, and never had been
The chapel had been demolished so that it could be rebuilt
The innkeeper told him that knights never really did that
He changed his mind and chose the stable instead
items.hint: The host had an answer ready, and said such a thing was allowed in cases of necessity.
items.why: The chapel “had recently been demolished so that it might be rebuilt,” so he put his armor in a trough in the yard.

items.q: The last page of this week's first reading is a full-page picture. What does it show?
opts: Don Quixote fighting off the angry mule drivers with his shield
Don Quixote kneeling as the innkeeper dubs him a knight
Don Quixote marching up and down in the bright moonlight
Don Quixote riding away from the inn at first light
items.hint: Look at the caption printed under the picture. He is guarding something, all night long.
items.why: The caption reads: “For hours he marched up and down in the bright moonlight.” He is watching his armor.

items.q: His horse was only skin and bone, with as many points as a mariner's compass. What did Don Quixote believe it was?
opts: An ordinary farm horse that would have to do
A charger finer than the Bucephalus of Alexander
A horse he would have to sell before setting out
A hack that had been worn out by hard work
items.hint: The book tells you the plain truth about the animal and then tells you what it “appeared to him” to be. Those are two different things.
items.why: Believed: a charger superior to Alexander the Great's famous horse. Really: skin and bone. A clean evidence row for your table — page 4.

items.q: Who was Aldonza Lorenzo really, and what did Don Quixote make of her?
opts: A princess he had met at court, whom he renamed for her beauty
His niece, whom he renamed so she would sound grander
A lady who wrote to him, whom he renamed Dulcinea del Toboso
A farmer's daughter, whom he renamed Dulcinea del Toboso
items.hint: She did not seem to know or care anything about him. He needed a lady because a knight-errant without one was like a body without a soul.
items.why: Really: a good-looking farmer's daughter who barely knew him. Believed: the lady of his heart, worth a princess's name. Page 6.

items.q: He reached an inn just before nightfall. What did he believe he was seeing?
opts: A monastery where the monks would give him food and a bed for the night
A castle with four towers, silver spires, a drawbridge and a moat
A shepherd's hut of the kind he had been looking for all day
The great stone house of a giant he would have to fight
items.hint: Everything he saw was tinted and transformed by the nonsense he had gathered from his books.
items.why: Believed: a castle out of a romance. Really: an ordinary roadside inn. This is the strongest single row you can put in the table — page 8.

items.q: A pig-driver blew his horn to call his herd in from a field. What did Don Quixote make of it?
opts: A warning that robbers were somewhere near
A bell calling the guests in to their supper
A trumpet announcing his arrival
A church bell ringing in a village nearby
items.hint: He had been waiting at the door of what he thought was a castle, expecting a dwarf or a page to do exactly this from the battlements.
items.why: Believed: his herald. Really: a pig-driver calling pigs. He did not pause to check — he “at once” recognized it as his signal. Page 8.

items.q: Two young women were standing by the door of the inn. What did he take them for?
opts: Servants he could send to announce him
Two beautiful damsels
Prisoners of the lord of the castle
Travellers he ought to warn about robbers
items.hint: They were on their way to Seville and stopping for the night. He spoke to them as though they were highborn ladies.
items.why: Believed: damsels at a castle gate. Really: two travellers who were alarmed by him. Page 8.

items.q: What did the landlord actually understand about his guest?
opts: That he was a real knight travelling the roads in disguise
That he was a rich man who would pay very well for a good room
That he was dangerous and should be turned away at once
He readily made out the kind of madness the stranger suffered
items.hint: The host knew a great deal about the romances of knights-errant, and he had guests to entertain.
items.why: This is your counter-evidence. Everyone else can see what is really going on — which makes Don Quixote's belief stand out all the more. Page 9.

items.q: A mule driver came to the trough to move the armor. What did Don Quixote do, and why?
opts: He asked him to wait until morning, because the vigil was nearly over
He knocked him out with his lance, because the armor was under guard
He let him take it, because he had finished his watch
He called for the landlord, because he was not allowed to fight
items.hint: The driver only wanted to fetch water for his mules. A second one came along later and got exactly the same treatment.
items.why: He was not pretending. He was keeping a real vigil over real armor and struck a real blow. Strong evidence that he believes it — page 11.

items.q: Which of these would be the strongest evidence that Don Quixote truly believes his adventures are real?
opts: He gave his horse a grand name after thinking about it for four days
He knocked a man out cold to protect armor he was guarding
He read a great many books about knights and chivalry
He chose a new and more impressive name for himself
items.hint: Think about the mule driver he knocked out with his lance. Which choice costs somebody something real?
items.why: He knocked a man out with his lance to guard his armor. Acting on a belief, at real cost to a real person, is far stronger evidence than liking the idea of knights. That is the reasoning the Explain column wants.

items.q: In RACES, what does the C step ask you to do?
opts: Compare this book with another story that you have read
Give specific evidence and the printed page numbers
Check your spelling and your punctuation carefully
Copy out the question at the top of your answer
items.hint: Look at the toolkit table on page 2 of your guide. It is the step that puts numbers in your answer.
items.why: Cite: “Give specific evidence and printed page numbers. Include the number of examples requested.”

items.q: The big question asks for three examples. How many do you have to cite?
opts: One good one is enough if you explain it well
Two, with the third saved for the final essay
Three
As many as you can fit on the page
items.hint: The Cite row says to include the number of examples requested. The evidence table has exactly that many rows.
items.why: Three. The guide says to include the number of examples requested, and the evidence table gives you three rows for them.

items.q: When should you use quotation marks?
opts: Whenever you mention something that happened in the book
Only when you copy the author's exact words
Every time you give a page number
Whenever you are writing about a character's speech
items.hint: Your detective habits say this in one line, just after the part about paraphrasing.
items.why: “Use quotation marks only when you copy the author's exact words.”

items.q: You put something from the book into your own words. Do you still need a page number?
opts: No, page numbers are only needed for direct quotations
Only if the detail comes from the home reading
Only if your teacher asks for one
Yes — a paraphrase still needs a page citation
items.hint: This is the line directly before the one about quotation marks.
items.why: “A paraphrase needs a page citation.” Putting it in your own words does not make it yours.

items.q: Which of these is a theme, rather than just a topic?
opts: Imagination, and what it can do to a person's mind
Believing something strongly does not make it true
The adventures of a man who reads too many books
Knights, and the stories people tell about them
items.hint: Your guide says a theme is a complete message about life, not a single word.
items.why: A theme is “a complete message about life, rather than a single topic word.” The others are topics or a plot summary — none of them says anything about life.

items.q: Your detective habits tell you to explain a detail. What does that mean?
opts: Retell what happened in as much detail as you possibly can
Say what it shows, rather than only saying what happened
Describe what the picture on the page looks like
Write down every word that the character said
items.hint: The guide puts it as a contrast: explain a detail instead of doing one other thing.
items.why: “Explain a detail instead of only retelling it.” That is exactly what the third column of the evidence table is for.

items.q: Your Week 1 page defines chivalry. What is it?
opts: A code of conduct associated with knights
The armor and weapons a knight carried into battle
A long journey made on horseback in search of adventure
The ceremony in which a man is made a knight
items.hint: Your guide gives it in a few words under “Words for the journey.” The book's grey circle on page 2 says much the same thing.
items.why: Your guide: “chivalry = a code of conduct associated with knights.” The book calls it the ideals of medieval knights — gallantry, honor and courtesy.

items.q: Your Week 1 page defines squire. What is one?
opts: A knight who has won many battles
A nobleman who owns a great deal of land
A knight's helper
A horse trained to carry a knight in armor
items.hint: You have not met one yet in pages 1 to 12. Watch for the man who takes this job once Don Quixote has set out properly.
items.why: Your guide: “squire = a knight's helper.” Sancho Panza takes that role later on.

items.q: Your Week 1 page defines irony. What is it?
opts: A meaningful contrast between expectation and reality
A funny remark made at somebody else's expense in a story
A story that teaches a lesson about life
A word that sounds like the thing it describes
items.hint: It is about the gap between what somebody expects and what is really so. This whole book runs on it.
items.why: Your guide: “irony = a meaningful contrast between expectation and reality.”

items.q: Which moment in pages 1–12 is the best example of irony?
opts: He spends four whole days deciding what he ought to call his horse
He sells good cropland so that he can buy himself more books
He sets out before daybreak so that nobody will see him go
He destroys his own visor, rebuilds it, then refuses to test it
items.hint: Look at what he does with the visor after he lines the cardboard with iron. He declares it strong without risking any more experiments.
items.why: He proved the visor useless with one stroke, then made certain never to prove it again. He expects to be a great knight; the reality is cardboard and strips of iron. Page 4.
